newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - UK demand grows for "fair-trade" coffee.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - UK demand grows for "fair-trade" coffee.

text.p: Sales are booming for the British company Cafedirect's "fairly-traded" coffee as public demand grows for ethical trading practices.

The message on every label of Cafedirect is simply this. "You get excellent coffee, they get a better deal." Cafedirect, started in 1991, is the flagship of Britain's fair trade movement which backers say reconciles profit with conscience and ethics.
"Cafedirect is a brand, it is the concept of direct, fair trading with Third World coffee farmers," says Humphrey Ping, Cafedirect's marketing manager.

"We are in this business to raise the issue and be part of a process that delivers significant improvement in conditions to a significant number of growers and we want that impact to go on growing," he said in a recent interview.
Cafedirect, as its name implies, buys coffee directly from small farmer co-operatives in Latin America and Africa, cutting out the middlemen.
It said farmers are guaranteed a minimum price of $1.26 per pound (500 grams) for arabica coffee beans and $1.06 for robusta coffee to cushion against any sharp falls in world prices.
They are also offered pre-payments of up to 60 percent of the minimum prices and a guaranteed 10 percent premium above prevailing market prices.
Despite having a price premium in the supermarket of five to 10 percent, a company official said the product has been selling very well.
Within the retail sector, Cafedirect estimates that it has won three percent of Britain's multi-million-pound roast and ground coffee market and two percent of the instant coffee market.

The coffee is available in more than 1,400 supermarkets across the country. The company's sales are expected to grow by 24 percent in 1996/97 (March/April) over 1995/96, Ping said, without giving the value.
"We are growing faster in freeze-dried instant and it's encouraging because that's a much bigger market," he said. Instant coffee makes up about 90 percent of the UK's coffee market.
Cafedirect started by importing three container loads of coffee in 1991. Since then, the company has sold some 162 million cups of coffee to consumers.
Cafedirect is founded by four organisations -- Oxfam Trading, Equal Exchange Trading, Traidcraft and Twin Trading.
The company buys coffee from 14 producer groups in Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nicaragua, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda.
Ping said the number of coffee-growing families involved has had more than doubled to 480,000 over the years.

He said small farmers were frequently cheated out of their earnings either through crop weighing methods or by being offered unfairly low prices. Looking ahead, Cafedirect is expanding its wings beyond British shores, taking the business initially to France and Switzerland. "We are carrying out market testing at the moment in Scandinavia," he added.
